What topic could you discuss in depth, given an engaged conversation partner?

The Walking Dead and Game of Thrones especially if the person has read all the source material for each.

My focus of study is around food science / safety on a microbiological level, so I often like to engage people on topics such as food additives, GMOs, treatment of animals, but usually I end up getting preachy with these topics if the conversation partner is uninformed.
To kind of combine those topics, do you notice any parallel Issues around food in either universe? GoT having a pseudo midieval timeframe and WD a modern but almost post-apocalyptic one?

Not really any parallel issues, but I read a great theory that says the reason GRRM includes such vivid descriptions of food early in the series so that when winter rolls around we'll begin to notice a distinct lack of these descriptions, implying the scarcity of these luxuries.

In the walking dead, around S3 of the show, I pointed out how they would need to begin planting crops to avoid food-borne illnesses from expired products, which they interestingly enough addressed early in S4. I think you have to take a lot of liberties with food in a post-apocalyptic setting. Vitamin C deficiency would be a big problem due to lack of fresh fruit, however broccoli and the skin of a potato contain as much Vit-C as a glass of orange juice. Also rice would be a huge post-apocalyptic food due to its high amount of essential amino acids, which is why you find it paired with beans and meats (to complete the rest of those amino acid requirements). Kirkman has addressed how much later in the comics than where the show is, how are people drinking coffee? He points out (correctly) that instant coffee has an incredibly long shelf life. Along this line, thermally-processed canned goods (done properly and kept out a extremely hot environment) can last for up to three years after their canning date. Honey is the only food product that never truly expires (yes twinkies can and will expire at some point, sorry Family Guy fans). A lot of foods like sauerkraut can resist most microbial growth simply due to their acidity, but will not last as long as canned/thermally procesesed foods.
Astrophysics, quantum mechanics, cosmology, M theory, etc. Honestly anything though.
Definitely topics above my head, but what have you learned about that you wish more people understood?

The Big Bang Theory. Everyone is prone to ask what came before the Big Bang. How can something come from nothing? In reality time is also dimension that exploded out in the theorized beginning. No time existed, therefore beginning and end are non-entities. It is not like exhaling having never drawn breath, it is no lungs at all.
It's interesing to think about, because it's very difficult for most people to really conceive "nothingness"
It is difficult for even the greatest minds. I find the best comparison would probably be our consciousness before birth. It is remarkable the reflection we share with the universe.

To add to that, the God as first cause argument, and how a conscious, all powerful entity coming from nothing seems more unlikely than a universe arising from nothing. Somehow "where did God come from?" rarely ends up as a followup when people claim that God created everything.
The conversations follow a similar path in many ways. Almost interchangable oddly enough.

True. The question really becomes "which is more likely?" To me, I am more comfortable with everything being devoid of inherent purpose and meaning, simply following physical laws that seem consistent enough even if we don't understand them. It seems like a conscious creator is only necessary if you have the psychological need for there to be one. I can't really conceive of a physical need for one. A random explosion of matter and energy from a void honestly seems less far-fetched than the concept of God, at least to me. That's how I justify atheism in the face of uncertainty.

The paradox comes in M theory where an infinite number of universes exist. Infinity would allow the possibility of an all powerful being to exist unless no lack of or excess of natural law in any way ever allows it. If that is the case, it break free dimensionally and supercede all natural laws.

Craziness. I guess we will see if the Hadron Collider proves interuniversality in January on restart.

I find the concept of infinite universes hard to believe. I don't think infiniite space and infinite time implies that all possible universes exist. It's a strange concept.

I guess I believe in multiple universes but not all possible universes, if that makes sense.

The seemingly impermeablity of membranes holding us dimensionally would allow for finite math and therefore observable universes to exist. Possibly in more dimensionally complex membranes observation is higher or impossible all together. It could be another case of we can observe and compute because we can. In a universe we couldn't the question couldn't be asked.

Our brains are evolutionally designed for survival. We see at the size and dimension we do for that reason. So if there is a meaning of life beyond us it isn't survival. What does that mean philosophically?

I think we may end up where most people end up intuitively: that life has the meaning that we give it, no more, no less. It may even be that life is important because we were evolutionarily designed to think of it as important, and people who take its emptiness or meaninglessness too far select themselves right out of the gene pool.

I almost think a higher level meaning would be irrelevant in a certain sense. What meaning can life have outside the context in which it lives? I honestly think meaning is only possible for an individual life when it stops searching for meaning in a more universal sense.

At first glance I have the tendancy to agree with you. The scale we live in is the one in front of our face. Maybe the answers to the hardest questions are there as well.

I will continue the search for it nonetheless.

As will I. I'm believing more and more lately that the answer has to be personal, because the question is personal.

Pretty unscientific to look at it that way, but alas...

GMOs and why most aren't so bad

This is definitely one of those topics prone to angry thought germs. I notice people tend to latch on to Monsanto and completely ignore the other positive aspects of GMO research. What positives can you share for readers less familiar with the topic?

My go to is Golden Rice. There is a huge problem of Vitamin A deficiency in many parts of the world and they engineered rice to have beta-carotene, resulting in the color of the rice being yellow.

A virus was destroying the crops because of the lack of diversity, so they modified some crops to be resistant to the virus which would have likely to otherwise continue its path of destruction.
